newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Southeast spot power prices rise after storm.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Southeast spot power prices rise after storm.

text.p: Spot electricity prices in the southeastern U.S. rose Friday after Hurricane Fran pounded the Carolina region overnight and ravaged a significant amount of transmission and distribution assets, industry sources said.

Although evacuation of coastal residents and cool temperatures dropped power demand in the region, movement of electricity in the Southeast was restricted because several low-cost power producers sustained severe storm-related damages to their transmission equipments, traders said.
Lower supply availability for at least the next couple days forced spot power prices higher, they said.

Within the Southeastern Electric Reliability Council (SERC), peak, non-firm power for the weekend was assessed at $18.00-$20.00 per megawatt hour (MWh) and for Monday $22.50-$23.50, compared with a midweek range of $18.00-$21.50.
Off-peak weekend electricity in SERC was quoted in the $12.00 area.
At the Georgia/Florida border, peak, non-firm power prices for the weekend were valued at $23.50, and off-peak weekend prices at $17.00-$18.00.
In the Florida pennisula, non-firm, peak electricity prices for weekend delivery were quoted at $24.00-$25.00, and for Monday delivery in the $28.00 area.
The spot Florida power prices were strong this week due to outages of two nuclear plants in the state.
Florida Power & Light Co's 839 megawatt (MW) St Lucie 1 nuclear power plant will likely operate at reduced power for the next two weeks, while it repairs one of the unit's main transformer.
Florida Power Corp's 825 MW Crystal River 3 nuclear unit remained shut because of lube oil leak. The utility said it did not set a restart date for the station.
